node.label: Julia Kristeva
node.date_label: La Révolution du langage poétique (1974) · Pouvoirs de l’horreur (1980; English 1982) · Étrangers à nous-mêmes (1988; English 1991)
node.description: In Pouvoirs de l’horreur (1980; Powers of Horror, 1982), Julia Kristeva explains abjection as the exclusion through which a subject establishes precarious boundaries between self and other. In La Révolution du langage poétique (1974), she treats bodily drives and rhythms, the semiotic, as interacting with the symbolic organization of language. Her work connected psychoanalysis with textual interpretation and feminist debates over identity and historical time. Hayden White reviewed Desire in Language (1980) in the Journal of Modern History (1982). Reception was also critical: as Kathleen Lennon recounts, Judith Butler’s Gender Trouble (1990) questions whether Kristeva’s apparently precultural maternal drives are themselves culturally produced. Nicolás Pastor-Berdún reconstructs Spivak’s 1981 objection that Des Chinoises (1974) opposes homogeneous pictures of China and the West. In “Women’s Time” (1979; English 1981), Kristeva distinguishes three generations of feminism and favours one that neither fixes identity nor neutralizes sexual difference.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Sèméiotikè: Recherches pour une sémanalyse (1969); La Révolution du langage poétique (1974); Des Chinoises (1974); “Le Temps des femmes” (1979; “Women’s Time,” translated by Alice Jardine and Harry Blake, 1981); Pouvoirs de l’horreur (1980; Powers of Horror, translated by Leon S. Roudiez, 1982); Desire in Language (English essay collection edited by Leon S. Roudiez, 1980); Histoires d’amour (1983; Tales of Love, 1987); Étrangers à nous-mêmes (1988; Strangers to Ourselves, 1991); Le Génie féminin, tome I: Hannah Arendt (1999; English translation by Ross Guberman, 2001).
node.scope_note: The complete 2011 Lacan interview, selected 2015 lecture passages and the 2025 interview’s third answer were read. Major monographs, “Le Temps des femmes” and its English translation (read through the Stanford Encyclopedia’s account), Butler’s Gender Trouble, Spivak’s 1981 essay, and White’s full review remain unread. Abjection and the imaginary father are read through named reference scholarship; White’s assessment is limited to a publisher-reproduced excerpt. The China critique and kinship debt are mediated through Pastor-Berdún’s selected pages.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Roland Barthes, à contre-courant” (2015), Kristeva recalls introducing intertextuality to Barthes, who developed it in his reading of Balzac in S/Z.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author’s 2 December 2015 lecture, section 1, concluding paragraph beginning Nos recherches se sont une fois de plus croisées: “l’intertextualité que je lui avais apportée.” Direction records Kristeva’s retrospective attribution. Barthes’s S/Z and L’Étrangère are unread; no claim that their theories were identical.
proposed_edges.map_label: Intertextuality as a resource for S/Z

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2011 interview “Lacan ou la portée historique de la psychanalyse,” Kristeva identifies Lacan’s Encore as a resource for her dialogue with his ideas about feminine enjoyment in Thérèse mon amour (2008).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete 2011 author-posted interview, answer to Que reste-t-il de Lacan d’un point de vue théorique aujourd’hui, paragraph beginning Sans avoir systématisé: “Je dialogue avec ses positions dans mon livre Thérèse mon amour.” The next sentence names Encore. The book and seminar are unread. This is a declared textual debt; no analyst, supervisor or seminar-attendance relationship is asserted.
proposed_edges.map_label: Encore as a resource for Thérèse mon amour

proposed_edges.relationship: In Gender Trouble (1990), Butler challenges Kristeva’s treatment of maternal drives as prior to culture, asking whether those drives are themselves culturally constituted, as Kathleen Lennon recounts (2010).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Lennon, archived Winter 2013 SEP entry, section 4, paragraph beginning Kristeva’s account of the maternal body has, however, come under attack. Cites Butler 1990, pp. 88, 92–93, and the need to examine “specific power relations.” Named-reader route; Gender Trouble unread. Does not imply rejection of every Kristevan concept.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Hannah Arendt (1999; English translation 2001), Kristeva interprets Arendt through the relation between life and thought and freedom as beginning, an interpretation she explains in her 2025 interview on the Female Genius trilogy.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author-posted 30 March 2025 interview, Q3 and answer: her account of Arendt links freedom to “a new beginning.” Read alongside Columbia’s description and contents, especially Life as a Narrative, and the official bibliography’s 1999 French date. Full book unread. This is Kristeva’s reading of Arendt, not a claim of personal collaboration.
proposed_edges.map_label: Reads freedom as beginning and renewal

proposed_edges.relationship: In “French Feminism in an International Frame” (1981), Spivak criticizes the homogeneous China/West opposition in Kristeva’s Des Chinoises (1974), as Nicolás Pastor-Berdún reconstructs (2026).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pastor-Berdún, p. 8, section 5, paragraph beginning Como señalan autoras feministas decoloniales; cites Spivak 1981, pp. 157–158 and 164. Phrase: “retrato homogéneo y unitario.” Spivak’s essay and Kristeva’s book unread. His p. 2 n. 3 says Spivak does not use the term orientalism; that label is therefore not attributed directly to her.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Des Chinoises (1974), Kristeva draws on Lévi-Strauss’s kinship analysis for her account of early Chinese social organization, as Pastor-Berdún shows through a textual comparison (2026).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pastor-Berdún, p. 9, section 6, from Kristeva (2016, p. 57) reconoce to the paragraph ending Lévi-Strauss: “incorporando sin embargo la corrección dualista.” He separates Granet’s hypotheses from Lévi-Strauss’s revisions. Original texts unread. The resource is documented; the historical validity of Kristeva’s reconstruction is not endorsed.

proposed_edges.relationship: La Révolution du langage poétique (1974) distinguishes the bodily rhythms and drives of the semiotic from the symbolic organization of language, treating them as interacting parts of signification.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Kristeva’s 2015 Barthes lecture, section 1 closing paragraph, contrasts “mode sémiotique” and “mode symbolique” and names the 1974 book; the Holberg committee citation describes their interaction. Leeb and Zakin’s section 4.2 supplies a scholarly reading. Book unread; this is a contribution to language and subject-formation debates, not a claim about adoption by all historians.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Le Temps des femmes” (1979; “Women’s Time,” 1981), Kristeva distinguishes three generations of feminism and favours a third that neither fixes identity nor neutralizes sexual difference, as the Stanford Encyclopedia’s account of psychoanalytic feminism explains (2025).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at verification on the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry by Claudia Leeb and Emily Zakin, section on 'Women's Time': three generations of feminism, the third following 'neither the path of fixing identity nor the path of neutralizing difference'. The 1981 article is recorded bibliographically (Signs 7:1, 13–35; French original 1979) and was not read on a permitted route.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Histoires d’amour (1983; Tales of Love, 1987), Kristeva reworks Freud’s account of primary paternal identification into an account of a loving imaginary father preceding symbolic law, as Claudia Leeb and Emily Zakin explain (2025).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Claudia Leeb and Emily Zakin, “Psychoanalytic Feminism,” substantive revision 3 October 2025, section 4.2, paragraph beginning “Although symbolic violence is integral”: links Kristeva’s imaginary father to Freud’s account in The Ego and the Id. Histoires d’amour and Freud’s book remain unread. The endpoint freud denotes the existing Freudian psychoanalysis tradition.
proposed_edges.map_label: Reworks primary identification in Tales of Love

proposed_edges.relationship: In Justice Interruptus (1997), Nancy Fraser criticizes Kristeva's discourse theory for reducing varied forms of human communication to a symbolic language system, as Sullivan and Tarver explain.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the substantive discussion in section 10.2 and its bibliography. This is Sullivan and Tarver's attributed account of Fraser's criticism; Justice Interruptus itself remains unread. The claim is limited to that account.
proposed_edges.map_label: Criticizes the reduction of communication to a symbolic system

proposed_edges.relationship: Kristeva's theory of abjection in Pouvoirs de l'horreur (1980; Powers of Horror, 1982) became a resource for analysing spatial exclusion and marginalised communities in critical geography, as Ben Campkin explains in 2013.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read manuscript pp. 14–15 and notes 53–59. The body develops the application; note 58 specifies its disciplinary scope. Target mapping is to the node's critical spatial studies strand. Original and translation years checked in Kristeva's bibliography; the book remains unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Abjection as a resource for analysing spatial exclusion
